q: At December 31, Archer Corp. owned equipment with a book carrying amount of $600,000 and a tax basis of $450,000. The enacted tax rate for all future years is 21%. What deferred tax amount should Archer report for the equipment?
choices: $31,500 deferred tax liability
$150,000 deferred tax liability
$15,750 deferred tax liability
exp: Book basis exceeds tax basis by $150,000, a taxable temporary difference that produces future taxable amounts: $150,000 x 21% = $31,500 DTL (ASC 740-10-30). The $150,000 answer is the temporary difference itself, not its tax effect.

q: Bell Co. reported pretax financial income of $500,000. It included $20,000 of tax-exempt municipal bond interest, and tax depreciation exceeded book depreciation by $40,000 (an originating difference). The enacted tax rate is 25% for all years. What is Bell's total income tax expense?
exp: Taxable income is $500,000 - $20,000 - $40,000 = $440,000, so current tax is $110,000; the deferred tax expense is $40,000 x 25% = $10,000; total = $120,000 (equivalently, 25% x $480,000 of income excluding the permanent difference). The $110,000 answer omits deferred tax expense.

q: At the end of Year 1, Carver Inc. has a $300,000 taxable temporary difference that will reverse equally in Years 2, 3, and 4. Enacted tax rates are 25% for Year 2, 22% for Year 3, and 20% for Year 4. What deferred tax liability should Carver report at the end of Year 1?
exp: Deferred taxes are measured using enacted rates for the years the differences reverse: $100,000 x 25% + $100,000 x 22% + $100,000 x 20% = $67,000. The $75,000 answer applies the current rate to all years, ignoring enacted future rates.

q: Dunmore Co. had a deferred tax liability of $100,000 based on a $400,000 taxable temporary difference and a 25% rate. During the current year, legislation was enacted reducing the rate to 21% for all future years. Ignoring other changes, how should Dunmore account for the rate change?
choices: A $16,000 adjustment to beginning retained earnings
No adjustment until the temporary difference reverses
A $16,000 increase in income tax expense
A $16,000 decrease in income tax expense from continuing operations in the period of enactment
exp: Deferred taxes are remeasured when a rate change is enacted, with the effect in income from continuing operations: $400,000 x 21% = $84,000, a $16,000 reduction of the DTL and tax expense (ASC 740-10-35-4). Retrospective adjustment of retained earnings is not permitted.

q: Ellis Corp. has a deferred tax asset of $200,000. Based on available evidence, Ellis concludes it is more likely than not that 30% of the deferred tax asset will not be realized. What valuation allowance should Ellis record?
exp: A valuation allowance reduces the DTA to the amount more likely than not to be realized: $200,000 x 30% = $60,000, leaving a net DTA of $140,000. The $140,000 answer is the net realizable DTA, not the allowance.

q: Foster Inc. generated a $1,000,000 federal net operating loss in Year 1 (after 2020). In Year 2, its taxable income before the NOL deduction was $500,000. The tax rate is 21%. What is Foster's federal income tax payable for Year 2?
exp: Post-2020 NOL deductions are limited to 80% of taxable income: 80% x $500,000 = $400,000 used, leaving $100,000 taxable x 21% = $21,000. The $0 answer ignores the 80% limitation.

q: Gaines Co. took a tax position providing a $100,000 tax benefit and concluded it is more likely than not to be sustained on its technical merits. Management estimates the possible settlement outcomes as: $100,000 (40% probability), $80,000 (25%), $60,000 (20%), and $0 (15%). What tax benefit should Gaines recognize?
exp: The benefit recognized is the largest amount that is more than 50% likely to be realized on settlement: cumulative probability reaches 65% at $80,000 (40% + 25%). The $100,000 answer has only a 40% cumulative probability.

q: Hayden Corp. claimed a $50,000 tax deduction benefit on its return. Hayden concludes there is only a 40% likelihood the position would be sustained on its technical merits upon examination. What liability for unrecognized tax benefits should Hayden record?
exp: A position that fails the more-likely-than-not recognition threshold receives no benefit, so the entire $50,000 claimed is a liability for unrecognized tax benefits (ASC 740-10-25-6). Multiplying by the 40% probability confuses recognition with measurement.

q: Irwin Co. had income from continuing operations before taxes of $800,000 and a pretax loss from discontinued operations of $200,000. The tax rate is 25% for all items. Using intraperiod tax allocation, what should Irwin report as the loss from discontinued operations?
choices: $150,000 net of tax
$200,000 net of tax
$50,000 net of tax
$250,000 net of tax
exp: Intraperiod allocation reports discontinued operations net of its own tax effect: $200,000 - ($200,000 x 25%) = $150,000 loss, with continuing operations bearing $200,000 of tax. The $250,000 answer adds the tax effect rather than subtracting it.

q: Jasper Inc. has a $50,000 deferred tax liability and a $30,000 deferred tax asset, both related to the same tax-paying component and jurisdiction, with no valuation allowance. How should Jasper present these amounts on its classified balance sheet?
choices: A $30,000 current DTA and a $50,000 noncurrent DTL
A $20,000 net noncurrent DTL
A $30,000 noncurrent DTA and a $50,000 noncurrent DTL shown separately
A $20,000 net current DTL
exp: Under ASU 2015-17, all deferred taxes are classified as noncurrent, and DTAs and DTLs of the same tax-paying component within the same jurisdiction are offset: $50,000 - $30,000 = $20,000 noncurrent DTL. Current/noncurrent splitting is the superseded approach.

q: Kline Co. accrued $90,000 of warranty expense for book purposes this year and paid $30,000 of warranty claims, which are deductible for tax when paid. The enacted tax rate is 21%. What deferred tax amount arises from the warranty?
choices: $18,900 deferred tax asset
$6,300 deferred tax asset
$12,600 deferred tax asset
$12,600 deferred tax liability
exp: The $60,000 accrued but unpaid warranty liability will produce future deductions: $60,000 x 21% = $12,600 DTA. The $18,900 answer uses the total accrual instead of the unpaid portion, and a DTL would reverse the direction of the difference.

q: In December, Lane Corp. collected $120,000 of rent in advance for the following year; the rent is taxable when received. The enacted tax rate is 25%. How should Lane account for the tax effect at December 31?
choices: A $30,000 deferred tax liability
A $120,000 deferred tax asset
No deferred taxes, because it is a permanent difference
A $30,000 deferred tax asset
exp: Rent taxed before it is earned creates a book liability with a zero tax basis, which will produce future deductible amounts: $120,000 x 25% = $30,000 DTA. Treating it as a DTL confuses it with revenue recognized for book before tax.

q: Morse Inc. had pretax financial income of $1,000,000, which included $50,000 of nondeductible fines and $30,000 of tax-exempt interest. There are no temporary differences, and the statutory rate is 21%. What is Morse's effective tax rate?
exp: Taxable income is $1,000,000 + $50,000 - $30,000 = $1,020,000; tax of $214,200 / $1,000,000 pretax income = 21.42%. Permanent differences change the effective rate, so the statutory 21% is not the answer.

q: Norton Corp. owns 30% of Pine Co. and uses the equity method. Norton's share of Pine's undistributed earnings is $400,000, which it expects to receive as future dividends eligible for a 65% dividends-received deduction. The tax rate is 21%. What deferred tax liability should Norton recognize for the undistributed earnings?
exp: Assuming recovery through dividends, only 35% of the earnings will be taxed: $400,000 x 35% x 21% = $29,400 DTL. The $84,000 answer ignores the dividends-received deduction, and the indefinite reinvestment exception does not apply to domestic equity method investees.

q: Osborn Co.'s foreign subsidiary has $2,000,000 of undistributed earnings that Osborn has demonstrated will be indefinitely reinvested abroad. If remitted, incremental U.S. and withholding taxes would be $100,000. How should Osborn account for the potential tax?
choices: Record a $100,000 deferred tax liability
Record a $420,000 deferred tax liability
Record no deferred tax liability but disclose the unrecognized amount if practicable
Record a $50,000 deferred tax liability
exp: ASC 740-30-25-17 provides an exception for outside basis differences of foreign subsidiaries when earnings are indefinitely reinvested; no DTL is recorded, but the unrecognized DTL is disclosed if practicable. Recording $100,000 ignores the exception.

q: In a nontaxable business combination, Pratt Inc. acquired identifiable assets with a fair value of $500,000 and a carryover tax basis of $300,000. The tax rate is 25%. What is the effect of the related deferred taxes on the goodwill Pratt records?
choices: No effect
Goodwill decreases by $50,000
Goodwill increases by $200,000
Goodwill increases by $50,000
exp: A DTL of ($500,000 - $300,000) x 25% = $50,000 is recognized as an assumed liability in the acquisition, reducing net assets acquired and increasing goodwill by $50,000 (ASC 805-740). The $200,000 answer uses the basis difference rather than its tax effect.

q: Quincy Corp. reported pretax income of $200,000 in the first quarter, using an estimated annual effective tax rate of 24%. Year-to-date pretax income through the second quarter was $450,000, and the revised estimated annual effective rate was 23%. What income tax expense should Quincy report for the second quarter?
exp: Interim tax is computed year to date: $450,000 x 23% = $103,500 less first-quarter expense of $48,000 ($200,000 x 24%) = $55,500 (ASC 740-270). The $57,500 answer applies the new rate only to second-quarter income and skips the catch-up for the rate change.

q: During the year, Reyes Co.'s deferred tax liability increased from $40,000 to $55,000 and its deferred tax asset (with no valuation allowance) increased from $20,000 to $28,000. No deferred taxes relate to OCI or business combinations. What is Reyes's deferred tax expense for the year?
exp: Deferred tax expense is the net change in deferred tax balances: $15,000 increase in the DTL less the $8,000 increase in the DTA = $7,000. The $23,000 answer adds the DTA increase instead of treating it as a benefit.

q: At December 31, Sutton Inc. concluded that, based on a sustained return to profitability and projected future taxable income, a previously recorded $50,000 valuation allowance on its deferred tax assets is no longer needed. How should Sutton account for the release?
choices: Credit beginning retained earnings for $50,000
Credit other comprehensive income for $50,000
Reduce income tax expense by $50,000 in the current period
Amortize the $50,000 into income over five years
exp: A change in judgment about realizability of beginning-of-year DTAs is recognized in income from continuing operations in the period of change (ASC 740-10-45-20). Releasing directly to retained earnings would treat a change in estimate as a restatement.

q: Taggart Co. is evaluating whether it needs a valuation allowance for its deferred tax assets. Which of the following is negative evidence that weighs against realizing the deferred tax assets?
choices: A strong earnings history, excluding a nonrecurring loss
Existing contracts that will generate taxable income sufficient to realize the DTA
Appreciated assets whose built-in gains exceed the DTA
Cumulative losses in the most recent three years
exp: Cumulative losses in recent years are significant negative evidence that is difficult to overcome (ASC 740-10-30-21). The other items are examples of positive evidence listed in ASC 740-10-30-22.

q: Underwood Corp. had pretax financial income of $300,000. Tax depreciation exceeded book depreciation by $50,000, and warranty expense accrued for books exceeded warranty claims paid by $20,000. The tax rate is 21%. What is Underwood's current income tax expense?
exp: Taxable income = $300,000 - $50,000 excess tax depreciation + $20,000 nondeductible accrued warranty = $270,000 x 21% = $56,700. The $48,300 answer subtracts both differences, treating the warranty accrual as an extra deduction.

q: Vaughn Inc. recognized a $600,000 gross profit on an installment sale for book purposes this year. For tax purposes, it uses the installment method and collected one-third of the sales price this year. The tax rate is 21%. What deferred tax liability arises at year-end?
exp: Two-thirds of the gross profit, $400,000, remains to be taxed as collections occur: $400,000 x 21% = $84,000 DTL. The $126,000 answer applies the rate to the entire gross profit, ignoring the portion already taxed.

q: Whitley Co., a public company, recorded $300,000 of goodwill in a taxable acquisition of a business; the goodwill is deductible for tax purposes over 15 years. Goodwill is not amortized for book purposes and was not impaired in Year 1. The tax rate is 21%. What deferred tax amount relates to the goodwill at the end of Year 1?
choices: $63,000 deferred tax liability
$4,200 deferred tax liability
$20,000 deferred tax liability
exp: Tax amortization of $300,000 / 15 = $20,000 reduces the tax basis below book basis, creating a $20,000 taxable temporary difference x 21% = $4,200 DTL. The $0 answer would apply only to nondeductible goodwill, for which no DTL is recognized.

q: Yates Corp. had an $80,000 unrealized holding gain on available-for-sale debt securities during the year. The tax rate is 25%. How should the gain and its tax effect be reported?
choices: $80,000 in OCI, with $20,000 of tax expense in net income
$20,000 in OCI
$80,000 in OCI with no tax effect
$60,000 in OCI, net of a $20,000 deferred tax liability
exp: Tax effects follow the item: the $20,000 DTL ($80,000 x 25%) is charged to OCI, so OCI reports $60,000 net of tax (intraperiod allocation). Charging the tax to net income mismatches the tax with the item that created it.

q: Zane Co. accrues interest and penalties on its liabilities for unrecognized tax benefits. Under ASC 740, how may Zane classify these interest and penalties in its income statement?
choices: As either income tax expense or interest/penalty expense, based on an accounting policy election applied consistently and disclosed
Only as income tax expense
Only as interest expense and other operating expense
They are not accrued until assessed by the taxing authority
exp: ASC 740-10-45-25 allows a policy election to classify interest and penalties on unrecognized tax benefits either in income taxes or in interest expense and another appropriate expense line, applied consistently. They must be accrued when required by tax law, not when assessed.

q: Abbott Inc. has a $2,000,000 federal NOL carryforward, producing a gross deferred tax asset of $420,000 at a 21% rate. After weighing all evidence, management concludes it is more likely than not that only $1,200,000 of the NOL will be utilized. What valuation allowance is required?
exp: The unrealizable portion is $2,000,000 - $1,200,000 = $800,000 x 21% = $168,000 allowance, leaving a $252,000 net DTA. The $252,000 answer is the realizable amount, not the allowance.

q: Benton Co. is a lessee in an operating lease that is treated as a rental for tax purposes. At year-end, the right-of-use asset is $380,000 and the lease liability is $400,000; both have a tax basis of zero. The tax rate is 25%. What temporary differences and deferred taxes arise?
choices: None, because operating lease payments are deductible as paid
Only a $5,000 net deferred tax asset, with no gross amounts
A $95,000 DTL on the ROU asset and a $100,000 DTA on the lease liability
A $95,000 DTA on the ROU asset and a $100,000 DTL on the lease liability
exp: The ROU asset (book basis above zero tax basis) creates a taxable difference: $380,000 x 25% = $95,000 DTL; the lease liability creates a deductible difference: $400,000 x 25% = $100,000 DTA. Ignoring them because rent is deductible as paid overlooks the book balances recognized under ASC 842.

q: Carlton Corp. reported pretax financial income of $400,000, including $50,000 of nontaxable life insurance proceeds on a deceased officer and $10,000 of nondeductible premiums on officer life insurance. There are no temporary differences, and the tax rate is 21%. What is Carlton's current income tax expense?
exp: Taxable income = $400,000 - $50,000 nontaxable proceeds + $10,000 nondeductible premiums = $360,000 x 21% = $75,600. The $73,500 answer excludes the proceeds but forgets to add back the nondeductible premiums.

q: Dorian Co. had pretax income of $1,000,000 with no permanent or temporary differences other than a $30,000 federal research tax credit. The statutory rate is 21%. What is Dorian's effective tax rate?
exp: Tax = $1,000,000 x 21% - $30,000 credit = $180,000, an 18% effective rate; a credit reduces tax dollar for dollar. The 20.37% answer treats the credit as a $30,000 deduction from taxable income.

q: Effective January 1, Ellison Inc. terminated its S corporation election and became a taxable C corporation; no further approval was required. At that date, it had net taxable temporary differences of $500,000, and the enacted rate is 21%. How should Ellison account for the change in tax status?
choices: No deferred taxes until the differences reverse
Recognize $105,000 of deferred tax expense in income from continuing operations at the date of the change
Charge $105,000 directly to retained earnings
Recognize the $105,000 as deferred tax expense ratably over the reversal period
exp: Deferred taxes resulting from a change in tax status are recognized in income from continuing operations on the date the change becomes effective or is approved (ASC 740-10-25-32): $500,000 x 21% = $105,000. Charging retained earnings treats it as a retrospective change, which is not allowed.

q: Felder Co. is subject to a 21% federal rate and a 6% state income tax rate; state taxes are deductible for federal purposes. What combined statutory rate should Felder use to measure deferred taxes?
exp: Because state tax is federally deductible, the combined rate is 21% + 6% x (1 - 0.21) = 21% + 4.74% = 25.74%. Simply adding the rates (27%) ignores the federal benefit of the state deduction.

q: Garrett Corp. (U.S. parent) sold intellectual property to its wholly owned foreign subsidiary, recognizing a $1,000,000 taxable gain in the U.S. For consolidated reporting the IP has a book basis of $0, while its new tax basis in the subsidiary's jurisdiction is $1,000,000. The subsidiary's tax rate is 12.5%. Under current GAAP, what deferred tax asset is recognized in the buyer's jurisdiction?
choices: $0; the tax effects are deferred until the IP is sold to a third party
$210,000 recorded as a prepaid tax asset
exp: ASU 2016-16 requires current and deferred tax effects of intra-entity transfers of assets other than inventory to be recognized when the transfer occurs; the buyer's DTA is $1,000,000 x 12.5% = $125,000. Deferring the effects as a prepaid tax is now limited to inventory transfers.

q: Hastings Inc. sold inventory to its foreign subsidiary at a $200,000 profit, paying $42,000 of U.S. income tax on the sale. At year-end, the subsidiary still held all of the inventory. How should the $42,000 be treated in the consolidated financial statements?
choices: Deferred as a prepaid income tax asset until the inventory is sold to a third party
Recognized as income tax expense in the current year
Replaced with a deferred tax asset measured at the buyer's tax rate
Eliminated with no tax effect recorded
exp: Intra-entity inventory transfers remain an exception under ASC 740-10-25-3(e): taxes paid by the seller are deferred as a prepaid asset and no DTA is recorded for the buyer's basis difference. Measuring a DTA at the buyer's rate is the treatment for non-inventory transfers.

q: Inman Co. has a $100,000 capital loss carryforward that can be used only against capital gains. Inman has no capital gains, no unrealized capital gains, and no feasible tax-planning strategies to generate them. The tax rate is 21%. What net deferred tax asset should Inman report for the carryforward?
exp: A $21,000 gross DTA is recorded, but because there is no source of capital gain income, a full valuation allowance is needed, so the net DTA is $0. The $21,000 answer ignores the character limitation on realization.

q: Jarrett Corp. carried a $60,000 liability for unrecognized tax benefits related to a position under audit. During the year, Jarrett settled the matter with the taxing authority by paying $45,000. How should Jarrett account for the difference?
choices: A $15,000 gain in other income
A $45,000 increase in income tax expense
A $15,000 decrease in income tax expense
A $60,000 decrease in income tax expense
exp: Settlement for less than the recorded liability results in recognition of the $15,000 remaining benefit through income tax expense ($60,000 - $45,000). Reporting it as other income misclassifies an income tax item.

q: Kessler Inc., a public business entity applying ASU 2023-09, reported pretax income from continuing operations of $10,000,000 and has a 21% federal statutory rate. Which of the following reconciling items must be disclosed separately in its rate reconciliation because it meets the 5% quantitative threshold?
choices: A $90,000 nondeductible expense item
A $100,000 change in unrecognized tax benefits
A $50,000 effect of a cross-border tax law
A $120,000 effect of nontaxable income
exp: The threshold is 5% of income times the statutory rate: $10,000,000 x 21% x 5% = $105,000, so only the $120,000 item must be separately disclosed. Using 5% of pretax income ($500,000) would exclude every item.

q: Lawson Co. prepaid $40,000 of insurance for the next year. The full payment is deductible on this year's tax return, while for book purposes it will be expensed next year. The tax rate is 21%. What deferred tax amount arises at year-end?
choices: $8,400 deferred tax liability
$8,400 deferred tax asset
$40,000 deferred tax liability
exp: The prepaid asset has a $40,000 book basis and zero tax basis, so future book expense will not be deductible, creating a taxable temporary difference: $40,000 x 21% = $8,400 DTL. A DTA would apply only if the expense were recognized for book before tax.

q: In the current year (after 2020), Marlow Inc. incurred a $500,000 federal net operating loss. It had taxable income in each of the prior two years, and it is not a farming or insurance company. The tax rate is 21%. How should Marlow recognize the tax benefit of the NOL?
choices: As a $105,000 income tax refund receivable from carryback
As a $105,000 deferred tax asset for the carryforward, subject to a valuation allowance assessment
As no benefit until the NOL is used
As an $84,000 deferred tax asset, reflecting the 80% limitation
exp: Current federal law generally eliminates NOL carrybacks, so the benefit is a DTA for the carryforward: $500,000 x 21% = $105,000, evaluated for realizability. The 80% limitation affects when the NOL can be deducted, not the amount of the DTA.
